actions.justification: Mandatory first step - obtain comprehensive history including symptom onset, functional class, medication history, and triggers for decompensation in this HFmrEF patient.
Mandatory - perform complete physical exam to assess volume status, signs of congestion (JVD, rales, edema), and hemodynamic profile in this HFmrEF patient.
Mandatory diagnostic - ECG to evaluate for arrhythmias, ischemia, or conduction abnormalities that may be contributing to or causing heart failure with mildly reduced EF.
Mandatory lab to assess renal function, electrolytes, and glucose, essential in HFmrEF workup and guides medication dosing.
Mandatory biomarker to confirm diagnosis of heart failure, assess severity, and guide management decisions in HFmrEF.
Mandatory lab to evaluate for anemia or infection, both of which can precipitate or worsen heart failure.

Mandatory action within 60-minute deadline. Chest X-ray is essential to assess for pulmonary congestion, cardiomegaly, and pleural effusions in this patient with heart failure with mildly reduced EF (41-49%).
Mandatory action within 60-minute deadline. TSH is indicated to evaluate for thyroid dysfunction, which can precipitate or exacerbate heart failure and is a standard part of the heart failure workup.

With known HFmrEF (EF 41-49%), assessing the hemodynamic profile (wet/dry, warm/cold) guides appropriate therapy selection and helps determine whether diuresis, vasodilators, or other interventions are needed.
Patient has HFmrEF (EF 41-49%) - formal LVEF assessment is essential to guide therapy selection and determine eligibility for HF-specific interventions including GDMT optimization, ICD, and CRT.
Patient has HFmrEF with known reduced EF range (41-49%) - ICD candidacy assessment is indicated per HF guidelines once LVEF and NYHA class are confirmed.
CRT indication assessment is appropriate in HFmrEF patients to evaluate for cardiac resynchronization therapy based on QRS duration/morphology and LVEF.

Patient has HFmrEF (EF 41-49%). NYHA functional class assessment is essential to guide therapy decisions including ACE inhibitor/ARB/ARNI, beta-blocker, and MRA initiation, as well as eligibility for ivabradine and advanced therapies.

Assessing structural abnormalities (valvular disease, chamber dimensions) is important in HFmrEF to identify reversible causes and guide management decisions such as surgical or interventional correction.

With confirmed HFmrEF, evaluating candidacy for advanced therapies (CRT, LVAD, transplant) should be considered as part of comprehensive heart failure workup, particularly given the borderline EF range.

With HFmrEF (EF 41-49%), it is important to assess the optimal duration and appropriateness of guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) including beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, and MRAs to guide treatment planning.
Evaluate and initiate diuretic therapy if signs of volume overload/congestion are present in this HFmrEF patient, as diuretics are a key component of symptom management in heart failure.
Cardiac rehabilitation is recommended for stable heart failure patients to improve functional capacity, quality of life, and outcomes, and should be initiated once the patient is stabilized.
Patient has HFmrEF (EF 41-49%). After initial assessment and workup are complete, confirming that guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) is optimized is a key next step to improve outcomes.
ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) are indicated for HFmrEF to reduce morbidity and mortality per heart failure guidelines.
Beta-blockers are a cornerstone of GDMT for HF with reduced/mildly reduced EF (EF 41-49%) to reduce mortality and hospitalizations.

Patient has HFmrEF (EF 41-49%). Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (e.g., spironolactone/eplerenone) is indicated per guidelines to reduce morbidity/mortality in heart failure with reduced/mildly reduced EF, and has not yet been initiated.
If the patient remains in sinus rhythm with HR ≥70 bpm despite beta-blocker therapy, ivabradine is indicated per guidelines for HFmrEF/HFrEF to further reduce hospitalizations.

With diuretic therapy already initiated and CBC/BMP pending, reassess diuretic response; if inadequate decongestion, addition of a thiazide-type diuretic or metolazone for sequential nephron blockade may be warranted.
